Climate, as incredibly complex as it is, is still causal. It doesn't just change or fluctuate magically. One thing we do understand very well is a relatively unique characteristic of CO2 among the atmospheric gases. It tends to let in most forms of solar radiation, yet reflect back most forms of radiation that the planet radiates back. It effectively works to trap heat in. Venus being hotter than Mercury even though it's twice as far from the Sun is little more than a testament to it having a primarily CO2 atmosphere and Mercury having no atmosphere.

The reason this is important is because for the past million+ years our planet's atmosphere has had a balance of CO2 and was remaining relatively stable with a regular repeating variation. Then came the industrial revolution. Since then we've started creating new forms of CO2. Now the amount we're adding is relatively small (we're still talking millions of pounds of new CO2 being produced per second) in terms of the entire system's dynamics, but when you have a balanced scale any extra weight is going to obviously enough to tip it in one direction. Since then the overall levels of CO2 have been increasing very rapidly. In a matter of decades we've gone from the norm, to levels we haven't seen since before modern humans were even a species. Now that's going to absolutely have a causal impact on our atmosphere. And what we'd expect to see is a gradual increase in temperatures as CO2 levels increased. And that is exactly what we have observed.

So basically what we're seeing is exactly what we would expect to see as a causal effect of our impact. One could try to offer an alternative hypothesis, and the fossil fuels industry is aggressively funding any research attempts at doing so, but you would need to explain not only the warming but also why our increasing the CO2 levels would in turn not lead to an increase in warming. In any case such alternative research has to date proved unfruitful.

The short answer is statistics.

We have a pretty good understanding of how heat moves through the atmosphere currently, and we have built surprisingly accurate computer models that are getting more and more accurate each year. A lot of models are built, and the ones that make the best predictions are modified as time goes on, giving us more and more accurate models.

As an example, we understand how the antarctic circumpolar current works as a heat exchanger with currents in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. The Antarctic current flows around Antarctica, never going very far north, so the water stays cool year round. The big currents in the Atlantic and Pacific come into contact with the Antarctic current, which heats up the Antarctic current, and cools down the Atlantic and Pacific Currents. Basically this spreads the heat throughout the earth. This is what causes ice ages. Since the continents move over time, the land masses break up currents. We can change the position of the continents in the computer models, which give us new ocean currents that don't spread the heat around as effectively. The models that best describe our current world also accurately describe what we see in the rock record.

The Medieval Warm Period was centered on the North Atlantic. Globally temperatures were still normal for the period since the South Pacific was experiencing an unusually cold period during this time. The cause for the Medieval Warm Period is understood as well. There was a lull in volcanism, and an increase in solar radiation at this time, both of which are shown in the geologic record.

I'm going to assume that you mean "fluctuating" is a short term phenomenon, and "changed" is a long term shift. The climate has changed during different epochs on earth according to geological records, and fluctuates daily. The question is how does one tell from data? The answer is time series analysis. This a set of advanced statistical techniques that determine how much is random noise (fluctuating very locally), how much is periodic (fluctuating consistently over a time period), and how much is constant or has shifted. The topic is fairly deep, I recommend the book "Time Series Analysis and It's Applications with R Examples" by Shumway and Stoffer. It has several examples and exercises that use climate data sets.
